newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak credit tightening bites, perhaps too hard.
newsitem.headline: Slovak credit tightening bites, perhaps too hard.

text.p: Slovak central bank moves to rein in domestic lending are gradually working, but analysts warned on Wednesday that higher interest rates and a lack of liquidity could squeeze some banks too tightly.

Liquidity redistribution between banks is moderating lending and has boosted interbank money market rates to nearly 16 percent, making it costly for smaller banks to finance their activities, analysts said.
"The banks's lending activities have not stopped due to the current lack of liquidity, but they continue at a slower pace," said Jozef Bozek, an analyst at Tatra Banka.
Silvia Majlingova of CSOB Bratislava said loan expansion continues but it is partly funded by banks' foreign exchange assets being turned into crown assets.
In mid-July, the central bank approved a series of measures aimed at curbing domestic lending and getting banks to repatriate foreign assets to fund lending at home.
The measures included a Lombard rate hike to 15 percent from 13, a widening of the band for setting the daily crown rate and a rise in banks' minimum reserve requirements.

Though growth in key money supply, M2, slowed for two consecutive months to 19.0 percent year-on-year in September, loan expansion hit 19.2 percent year-on-year in September. The central bank's year-end target for M2 stands at 11.6 percent, and for loan expansion at 7.2 percent.

Largely consumption-oriented, the loan expansion was a response to the scrapping of credit limits by the central bank at the start of 1996, after positive inflation figures allowed an easing of monetary policy.
But as the central bank's measures begin to bite hardest, the banks have started to more or less reverse some of their lending activities, resulting in liquidity shifts between banks.

"As much as banks have been outstripping each other in extending loans, now some liquidity-sensitive banks will have problems to keep up the pace," Ivan Benda, a Treasury Director at Slovenska Sporitelna, told Reuters.

According to the measure effective December 31, the NBS requires banks to exclude foreign exchange assets held locally from their foreign exchange position, and include crown liabilities to banks outside Slovakia.
Banks must also reach a minimum ratio of foreign exchange assets and liabilities of 0.65 by December 31, rising in steps to at least 0.8 by June 30, 1997.

While analysts with smaller banks said they expected the market to suffer liquidity problems through to the end of 1996 and thus the current rates to hold, those with larger banks expected sufficient liquidity and a rate decline.

"The market overall is not so much short, the money is there, however along with a high interest rate factor, since some banks are forced to accept even higher interest rates," Emil Vitazka, a VUB Bank trader, said.
Central bank officials have said that while they are not pleased by the high rates, they did not expect them to stay at current levels over the longer-term.
